summary: Defines operational recommendations to ensure source-specific behavior within the 232/8 IPv4 range, which is designated for source-specific multicast. It is a Best Current Practice for PIM deployments.

eli5.summary: Some addresses are reserved for special group delivery. This explains rules for routers so those addresses work the way they should.

subtitle: Operational rules that keep the 232/8 multicast range strictly source-specific, with no shared trees and no RPs.

tldr.problem: The 232/8 range is reserved for source-specific multicast, but PIM-SM also supports shared trees through a Rendezvous Point, and MSDP announces sources between domains. Left alone, routers could deliver 232/8 traffic the wrong way.
tldr.mechanism: Routers and RPs are told to refuse registers, (*,G) joins, RP candidacy and MSDP Source Active messages for 232/8 groups, so only source-only trees ever carry that traffic.
tldr.outcome: Several sources can safely reuse the same 232/8 group address, and receivers get only the sources they asked for. This is a Best Current Practice (BCP 120).

today: RFC 4608 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 120) published in August 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why 232/8 Needs Operational Rules
sections.content:
The IP multicast group range 232/8 (232.0.0.0 to 232.255.255.255) is designated for Source-Specific Multicast (SSM). Ordinary PIM Sparse Mode (RFC 4601) relies on a shared Rendezvous Point (RP) tree to find active sources and to carry group-generic Any Source Multicast (ASM) traffic. Groups in 232/8 SHOULD use source-only trees instead, so no RP and no shared tree are needed. Active sources are discovered out of band.

Receivers' Designated Routers can join the shortest path tree to a source directly. The practices in this RFC make sure that shortest-path, source-only trees are what actually get used across multiple domains, and that data from sources sending to 232/8 groups never arrives over a shared tree. That avoids unwanted data and lets several sources use the same group address without conflict at the receivers.

The practices SHOULD prevent local sources from sending to the shared tree, prevent receivers from joining it, prevent RPs from being candidates for 232/8, and prevent remote sources from being learned or joined through MSDP.
sections.eli5: A special range of group addresses is meant for tuning in to one named sender. The rules stop routers from using the general meeting point for those addresses.

sections.title: A BCP About an Experimental Protocol
sections.content:
This document is a best current practice for a widely deployed Experimental protocol, MSDP (RFC 3618), which has no plan to advance to Proposed Standard. The RFC lists the reasons. MSDP was meant to be temporary until the IDMR working group, or later the BGMP working group, produced an inter-domain protocol, but neither produced one that could be deployed.

Other reasons given are scalability (readvertising everything you know every 60 seconds limits the state you can advertise), near-ubiquitous deployment of MSDP as the de facto inter-domain multicast protocol in the IPv4 Internet, and no consensus on reworking it. Protocols such as SSM and bi-directional PIM, plus embedded RP techniques for IPv6, further reduced the push for a replacement.

IETF policy says a BCP must not have normative references to Experimental protocols. Because MSDP will not be advanced, this document is a special case. The MBONED Working Group requested approval under the Variance Procedure of RFC 2026, and the IESG approved it after an additional 4-week IETF Last Call.
sections.eli5: The rules depend on a tool that was only ever labeled a trial, but everyone ended up using it. So the authors got special permission to write the rules anyway.

sections.title: Keeping Local Sources Off the Shared Tree
sections.content:
To eliminate shared trees for 232/8 groups while still coexisting with ASM in PIM-SM, the behavior of the RP and/or the Designated Router (DR) needs to be modified. Three things are prevented:

  • the DR sending 232/8 data encapsulated to the RP,
  • the RP accepting registers for 232/8 groups from the DR,
  • the RP forwarding accepted data down the (*,G) tree for 232/8 groups.
sections.eli5: A sender should not hand its 232/8 packets to the meeting-point router. The meeting point should refuse them and never pass them on.

sections.title: Keeping 232/8 Out of MSDP
sections.content: SSM does not need active source announcements through MSDP. Announcements arrive out of band, and the last hop router sends (S,G) joins directly to the source. To stop Source Active (SA) messages for 232/8 from spreading, an RP SHOULD never originate an SA for any 232/8 group, and SHOULD never accept or forward one.
sections.eli5: Because listeners already know which sender they want, no one needs to announce 232/8 senders to other networks. The routers simply stay quiet about them.

sections.title: Keeping Receivers Off the Shared Tree
sections.content:
Local PIM domain practice has to prevent receivers from joining the shared tree for 232/8 groups. That means the DR must not send (*,G) joins for those groups, and the RP must not accept them.

The RFC explains why partial enforcement is not enough. Within a domain, any last-hop router that does not block (*,G) joins may create unwanted (*,G) state toward the RP that intersects an existing (S,G) tree. A receiver on the shared tree could then get data, which breaks the source-specific service model of RFC 3569. So ALL routers in the domain MUST reject and never originate (*,G) joins for 232/8 groups.

If an ISP offers customers or others the use of its RP, the ISP SHOULD NOT allow (*,G) joins in the 232/8 range.
sections.eli5: If even one router lets a listener join the general channel for these addresses, that listener could hear senders it never picked. So every router has to say no.

sections.title: No RP Candidates for 232/8
sections.content:
Because SSM needs no RP, RPs SHOULD NOT offer themselves as candidates in 232/8. In practice this means RP and BSR announcements for 232/8 are prevented, all routers refuse RP delegations in the range, and RP functionality for the range is switched off on the RP.

The RFC notes that RPs typically announce themselves for 224/4, which includes 232/8. Advertising 224/4 or another superset is still acceptable, but it relies on routers silently ignoring the delegation for 232/8 and blocking sending or receiving on the shared tree. An RP SHOULD NOT be configured as a candidate RP for 232/8 or any more specific range.
sections.eli5: Meeting-point routers should not volunteer to host these special addresses. If they advertise a bigger range that includes them, other routers must ignore that part.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The practices introduce no new security issues to PIM-SM or to SSM or ASM operation. The risk comes from not following them. Section 2.3 describes what happens when last-hop routers do not comply, or when rogue hosts send PIM messages themselves: creating (*,G) state for a source-specific (S,G) could let a receiver get data it should not. The RFC says this can be mitigated by host-side multicast source filtering.
sections.eli5: If a router skips the rules, someone could listen to a sender they were not supposed to hear. Checking at the receiving computer helps catch that.

items.title: Local sources
items.text: Do not send to the shared tree.

items.title: Receivers
items.text: Do not join the shared tree.

items.title: MSDP
items.text: No SAs originated, accepted or forwarded.
